The funny thing is that once you get a kernel up and performing, and a network stack, you can pretty much make your own OS daily drivable. What would you need? A basic editor, GUI or not, a way to ssh into remote servers (so a ssh client, which will be tricky to write), and as many coreutils as you can write. Stay away from git, it's hard to implement from scratch. Make a useful File Manager and if you have a network, add a 4chan, Mastodon, Bluesky client so that you can get news from your "friends". Maybe a wget-like utility so you can dump pages into text files and read them Stallman-style. An email client is simple to build too, ~3k LoC including the POP3 and SMTP libs, but you'll need TLS for proper 2026 conenctions, so BearSSL will be your friend. Usenet client? That's another 2k lines over a NNTP library + client. IRC? Basic stuff, 1k LoC.
Lo and behold, your hobby OS is almost daily-drivable.

>>109909657
It's not hard if you get a proper scope: first you need a network driver, depending on what you plan to test, qemu or real hardware. Then a minimal netstack implementation would need ARP, Ethernet, minimal UDP, DHCP, IP and minimal DNS. No IP reassembly, no complex UDP, no ARP caching. If you want to go the static configuration route (you feed a static IP, netmask, gateway and DNS server(s) to your stack) you can skip DHCP, but DHCP is the fun part.
It's really not hard, but I've implemented 2 network stacks from scratch, so I may be biased.
Network stacks actually test your kernel's tasks/processes, isolation, memory management, so you can consider it as proper kernel testing too.

>>109920325
I am rewriting chunks of MAIDS OS, because I removed something from my language. I had a sugar syntax that looks like this:
foo:: ?{c, t, f};


Which desugars to:
foo:: [:: c t | [:: !c ] f ];


which can be rewritten as:
foo:: 
  c t
| !c f;


which I think looks nicer than the sugar syntax and is easier to write and easier to read.

Before the change, factorial could be expressed as:
factorial(*n)::
?{
        gt(*n, "0"),
        mul(*n, factorial(sub(*n, "1"))),
        ?{
                eq(*n, "0"),
                "1",
                "Cannot take factorial of negative number"
        }
};


Now I will just express it like this:
factorial(*n)::
  eq(*n, "0") "1"
| lt(*n, "0") "Cannot take factorial of negative number"
| gt(*n, "0") mul(*n, factorial(sub(*n, "1")));


Which looks nicer and doesn't involve counting commas, or braces, or indenting things, or mentally walking a tree to decide what code goes where, and trying to remember how conditions compose as you walk the tree.

The old syntax mimics a conditional, but MAIDS doesn't have conditionals, or booleans. It is goal-directed and backtracks.

>>109933690
Almost the whole language is memory safe, by construction. You just can't use pointers, access memory or interact with hardware. For the times when this is required, it is forced through a crutch instruction. So, all potentially unsafe code is 

 crutch("op", ...)


Unsafe stuff is limited entirely to crutch. Memory for the OS is split into four regions. If you try to write to a fixed spot which is out of bounds, the code won't compile. If you try to write to a computed spot, that won't compile unless you put a guard in front of it which proves that you are in bounds. If you do not include this guard, the compiler will attempt to prove it independently. If it can't, or it proves the value is out of bounds, compilation fails.

This looks interesting. Thank you for sharing it. It looks like it shares some similarities with MAIDS OS (MAIDS is homoiconic, but everything is a string instead of an object). The paper isn't really clear on how o-expressions differ from s-expressions. Lists are also objects, and you can used to to build any arbitrary object you can think of, so it seems like the two are equivalent, but maybe I am missing something, or the neo author just didn't explain it in detail. It basically looks like an attempt at making a modern LISP machine. My biggest contention with this is the same contention I had with the original LISP machines, that LISP itself has horrific syntax in all cases, and poor semantics in most cases. That anything it achieves and any nice property it has can be achieved or had with a more pleasantly designed language.

>This is how the physical world works. You start from an example and vary it. The blueprint is a fiction. In neo, the prototype is the first example, real, inspectable, and modifiable, and every other instance is a variation of it.
This kind of seems both grandiose and wrong? A blueprint is not "fiction". It is a set of instructions and specifications for how to make something. Just because you wouldn't find a blueprint for a skyscraper when walking around in a forest, doesn't mean the blueprint is a "fiction" or that it is somehow useless. It is still a set of instructions and specifications for how to build a skyscraper, and that is still useful.

Thank you again for sharing it. I think it would be interesting to see how this is developed. Has a system been constructed, or is it only a whitepaper right now?

Hello, I’m the author. There might be some misconceptions on my end. I’ll admit that.
The goal, simply put, is a homoiconic, n-dimensional, pure object system. I don’t understand Lisp, Smalltalk, Self, or even Haskell deeply enough yet to make a confident comparison, so I should probably be more careful with those claims.
What I’m imagining is a live object graph where spatial relationships and dimensionality are built into the model. Objects contain other objects, have their own behavior, and interact within that world. The live image is the world itself.
I initially described this as a step up from lists, but that’s probably misleading. Lisp can represent graphs too. The distinction I’m aiming for is making this spatial object model fundamental to the environment, rather than something you build on top.
So I’m not deliberately trying to recreate Lisp. In my head, it’s closer to rethinking Self with homoiconicity and a multidimensional live world at its core. I may still be misunderstanding parts of those systems, but that’s the direction I’m trying to explore.

As an osdever myself, let me offer you some advice:
- begin with x86, you will get actual Intel ME-free SCH, less or no microcode updates. For a hobby OS, adressing more than 4Gb of RAM is a non-issue, my OS runs in 32Mb of RAM with a web browser, ssh server, http server, development IDE + agentic coding assistant, all loaded at the same time. 4Gb is lol.
-HDMI/DP - fuck no, that's very very hard to work with, good luck getting documentation and datasheets for various converters.
- USB kb/mouse needs this: a generic USB controller driver, an EHCI or UHCI/OHCI driver (if you use newer hardware, goodluck with xHCI, it's proper cancer) and a USB HID driver. The whole triple package will take about .... 4 months to write. At least. Prepare to read about 1k documentation pages on USB specs.
- Ethernet is easy, that should be your initial target, to get your OS to the level where you can send packets using a virtual interface or a proper hardware device.
- I'd suggest x86 + PAE + NX bit for start, SMP later on if you have a multi-core or hyperthreading CPU.
- I 100% agree with you, qemu/bochs is not a target, it's very useful for testing, but proper hardware support is very important. It's a huge difference from having an OS which boots on qemu and an OS which boots on real hardware.
- regarding hardware targets, stick to laptops: ThinkPads, netbooks, old Pentium MMX portables, etc.
- everything depends on what you want your OS to achieve: do you want to daily-drive it? It's massive work, few years, LLMs can probably shorten that by a bit (I'm not using them and not interested to show them my code), but I bet it will ruin half the fun. I can understand using LLMs to get past the initial bootloader, kernel printf stages, because those are painful and you're looking at few weeks/months of work for nothing to show off. But I still advise anyone to write his or her own code, because in OSdev you can't skip stages.
